title: Splash: rock into water, which nothing could do before
question: Does the rock entry read as an impact? And is the crown big enough, or should it throw more?
context_md:
You said: *"I don't see any splash or difference in any of these, I think the issue is that you are testing with a disperse rain of sand instead of clumps of sand or rocks would be better."*

Your premise turned out to be backwards and your instinct turned out to be right, which is worth saying plainly.

**Backwards:** a splash needs air above the water it displaces, and a falling clump is the thing standing in that air. The engine refuses a splash site with anything over it -- so a denser clump makes the effect *disappear*, not appear. The scene's own comment says so, written before either of us looked at it.

**Right anyway:** a falling *boulder* reported no splash from anywhere, ever. The code that shoves whole columns of water out of a rigid body's way never told the splash system anything, so rock into water was completely silent. No amount of changing what I dropped would have found that.

A boulder now throws its crown where the water can actually go: up the sides, one column out from where it lands. It has to arrive with some speed, so a slab sliding off a ledge still enters quietly.

There was also **no scene that dropped rock into water**, so there is one now: a 600-cell slab held over an open pool by nothing, which the load model takes apart on the first frame.

| | droplets thrown |
|---|---|
| rock, before this change | **2** |
| rock, now | **33** |
| loose grains (the old scene) | 58, dribbled over 140 frames |

The two clips are the two different mechanisms, not two settings -- worth comparing for *shape*: the rock throws its 33 in a single burst over about six frames, the grains trickle theirs out the whole time.

The dark box in the rock clip is the scene, not a bug: the engine freezes what counts as "sky" on the first frame, and the slab is in the way, so its columns render unlit for the rest of the run.
